slides.headline: Rome’s Coastal Colony Became a Ruin
slides.subheadline: A trading post became an imperial foothold. Modern Tipaza began separately.
slides.svgBlueprint: Portrait viewBox 0 0 1080 1350. Paper background; 80px safe margins. Custom Brand masthead above orange kicker badge. Set headline in 72px bold serif across three lines; subheadline at 30px. One monumental broken-column silhouette occupies the lower half, interrupted by an orange fracture. Place two compact historical badges along the bottom rule. Issue badge upper-right. No diagrams, callout boxes, or connecting arrows.

slides.headline: Trade Became a Weapon of Conquest
slides.subheadline: Claudius turned a Punic trading-post into Rome’s military colony in Mauretania.

items.title: An imperial foothold
items.body: The colony served conquest of Mauretania’s kingdoms; commerce now shared the coast with military ambition.

items.title: A Christian center
items.body: Under later Roman governorship, three basilicas marked Tipasa’s importance as a Christian hub.

slides.svgBlueprint: Portrait 1080×1350 using the cover palette. Headline 60px; subheadline 30px. Stack two offset Surface cards beneath a minimal coastal contour. First card uses an orange military-standard silhouette; second uses a restrained basilica arch. Card bodies 28px, maximum three lines. Integrate one telemetry badge into each card’s lower edge, with fourth-century attribution explicitly attached to the population. Numerals maximum 48px. Decorative coastline is symbolic, not a geographic map.

slides.headline: The Name Outlived the Ancient City
slides.subheadline: Modern Tipaza’s founding does not establish uninterrupted survival of ancient Tipasa.

items.title: Settlement returns
items.body: The location was settled again in the nineteenth century; modern Tipaza was founded in 1857.

items.title: Do not collapse the dates
items.body: Ancient destruction and later resettlement belong to different chapters, not one intact urban life.

slides.svgBlueprint: Portrait 1080×1350; Paper background and 80px margins. Headline 60px. Center 1857 as a full-width 84px orange hero numeral with its founding label directly beneath. A wide blank band separates the date from a low-contrast archaeological baseline, visibly refusing continuity. Stack two compact editorial footnote cards below. Attach the 430 CE badge to the second card at 40px. Body text 28px; no continuous timeline connecting ancient and modern settlements.

slides.headline: Reconstruction Could Not Secure Permanence
slides.subheadline: Byzantine rebuilding reversed destruction, but Umayyad demolition later reduced the city to ruins.

items.title: Vandal destruction
items.body: Vandals destroyed Tipasa, breaking the Roman city’s trajectory.

items.title: Byzantine reconstruction
items.body: Byzantines reconstructed the city; destruction had not yet become its final condition.

items.title: Umayyad demolition
items.badge: the end of the seventh century
items.body: Umayyad forces demolished the city and reduced it to ruins.

telemetry.badge: the end of the seventh century
telemetry.label: Demolition

Orange broken segment for Vandal destruction; Ink repaired segment for Byzantine reconstruction; orange terminal break for Umayyad demolition. slides.kicker: THE VERDICT / A DIFFERENT KIND OF VALUE
slides.headline: The Foothold Became the Attraction
slides.subheadline: Ancient Tipasa survives as ruins, drawing visitors to a later coastal town.

items.title: Ancient Tipasa
items.body: Rome’s military colony did not survive intact; its remains preserve a broken imperial history.

items.title: Modern Tipaza
items.body: Founded in 1857, the later town draws tourists principally through the ancient ruins.

telemetry.label: Ancient city · fourth century · Stéphane Gsell

slides.closingQuestion: Are we seeing a surviving city—or another town’s inheritance?
